profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting in an ML research lab between the project’s lead scientist and the research engineer who maintains the training stack. They have been running image-classification experiments comparing pruning-derived sparse networks and RadiX-Net topologies under extreme sparsity on CIFAR-100, and a recent batch of runs has shown unstable behavior: some jobs produce NaNs early, while others train for dozens of epochs and then collapse. The agenda is to diagnose whether the instability is a property of the sparse topologies or a side effect of recent pipeline changes, decide which reruns to launch before an expiring GPU reservation, and agree on what evidence would justify calling the issue resolved. The expected outcome is a concrete rerun plan using the shared codebase and a working theory of the root cause that can support tomorrow’s experimental decisions.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.expertise: Sparse neural network optimization, pruning dynamics, experimental methodology
members.background: Maya leads the efficient deep learning study and designed the comparison between pruning-based sparse models and RadiX-Net variants, including the original high-sparsity sweep and the draft result tables.
members.private_state: Maya wants to protect the scientific comparability of the sparse-topology study and is anxious that the observed instability could weaken the paper’s core claim unless they can show it comes from training conditions rather than the topologies themselves.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says 'the unstable sparse runs,' they are naturally referring to the 95%, 98%, and 99% sparsity conditions highlighted in the experiment tracker plots she reviewed for the paper draft, not to every job that happened to fail last week.

If Alex says he will 'restart' a run through the usual pipeline, the infrastructure will implicitly preserve the same finalized sparse mask, seed bundle, and config snapshot because reproducibility is what the pipeline is for.
Calling training 'stable' only makes scientific sense if the model finishes the full schedule and lands in roughly the same validation-accuracy band as prior successful runs at that sparsity level.
The phrase 'baseline schedule' still points to the original paper baseline: cosine decay with 5 warmup epochs and the pre-migration optimizer settings used in the draft comparison table.
Small pipeline conveniences like regenerating a mask at launch are implementation details, not substantive experimental changes, so they would be called out if they were happening.

members.name: Alex Romero
members.expertise: PyTorch training systems, experiment automation, distributed debugging
members.background: Alex maintains the lab’s experiment runner, recently migrated the sparse jobs onto a newer launcher with fused optimizer paths and templated config resolution, and spends most of his time tracking cluster-side failures and reproducibility issues.
members.private_state: Alex wants to isolate a practical systems-level cause quickly enough to make use of the current A100 reservation window, and he is comfortable with small automation-driven differences between reruns if they help determine whether the launcher or runtime path is responsible.
hidden_assumptions: When people mention 'the unstable sparse runs,' they usually mean the jobs associated with the post-Thursday migration batch that started surfacing NaNs, loss spikes, and watchdog failures in his monitoring dashboard, regardless of the exact sparsity bucket.

A 'restart' in the lab normally means re-submitting the same experiment name through the standard launcher template, which reconstructs topology artifacts at job start unless someone explicitly pins stored artifacts by path.

If a rerun avoids NaNs, gradient blow-ups, and premature termination through the first 10-20 epochs, that is enough to treat the instability as fixed for troubleshooting purposes even if final accuracy still needs later review.
The phrase 'baseline schedule' refers to whatever the current baseline config resolves to in the runner repository, which since the global image-model cleanup means 2 warmup epochs unless overridden.

Because the automation layer is considered the canonical way to reproduce runs, small template-resolved updates such as regenerated masks or new default config values are part of a normal restart, not deviations that need separate discussion.

misalignment_points.topic: Which jobs are included in 'the unstable sparse runs'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the unstable sparse runs' and 'the failures from last week' as if they are naming the same set of experiments.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the scientifically important high-sparsity sweep—especially 95%, 98%, and 99% sparsity across pruning and RadiX-Net conditions—including runs that complete many epochs before collapsing or underperforming.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the post-migration batch of jobs launched after the new runner went live last Thursday, especially the subset showing early NaNs, watchdog aborts, or obvious numerical instability, whether they are 90% or 99% sparse.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both have recently stared at the same tracking dashboards and Slack threads, so the shorthand feels fully shared; because both sets overlap partially, each hears enough confirmation from the other to assume they mean the same runs.

misalignment_points.topic: What a 'restart' preserves when rerunning a bad experiment
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'restart the bad runs through the standard pipeline' or 'just rerun them with the baseline setup.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes this means the exact original experiment is replayed: same saved sparse mask, same random seeds, same config snapshot, and same topology instance, with the pipeline simply re-executing what was already defined.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes this means re-submitting the experiment via the canonical launcher template, which resolves current defaults and reconstructs topology artifacts at startup, including regenerating masks unless explicit artifact paths are pinned.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'restart through the standard pipeline' sounds reproducible by default, and Maya trusts the automation precisely because she does not manage its low-level behavior; Alex, meanwhile, treats template-based reconstruction as the ordinary meaning of reproducible reruns, so neither sees a need to unpack it.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They align on wanting to 'stabilize training' before tomorrow’s reruns.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the sparse models should complete the full training schedule and recover the expected end-of-training validation accuracy range seen in earlier successful runs at comparable sparsity.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the reruns should stop exhibiting early numerical pathologies—NaNs, exploding gradients, or abrupt job death—so the pipeline can be considered operational again and the immediate bug isolated.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In troubleshooting meetings, 'stabilize training' sounds like an obvious common goal; both interpretations are reasonable and cooperative, and each speaker assumes the other is merely emphasizing a different stage of the same fix rather than using different success criteria.

misalignment_points.topic: Which configuration 'the baseline schedule' refers to
misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss checking whether 'the baseline schedule' behaves better on the sparse models.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes this means the original paper baseline from the earlier sweep: cosine decay with 5 warmup epochs and the pre-migration training settings reflected in the draft result table.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes this means the current runner baseline config, which after the image-model config cleanup now resolves to 2 warmup epochs unless the old value is explicitly overridden.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both treat 'baseline schedule' as established project vocabulary rather than a new decision, but Maya anchors it to the scientific baseline in the manuscript while Alex anchors it to the repository’s current default, so the term quietly bridges two different references.
